section_title: How should we understand the vision of the lying spirit?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 19 Micaiah continued, “Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right and on His left. 20 And the LORD said, ‘Who will entice Ahab to march up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ And one suggested this, and another that. 21 Then a spirit came forward, stood before the LORD, and said, ‘I will entice him.’ ‘By what means?’ asked the LORD. 22 And he replied, ‘I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.’ ‘You will surely entice him and prevail,’ said the LORD. ‘Go and do it.’ 23 So you see, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all these prophets of yours, and the LORD has pronounced disaster against you.”

context_lines: Micaiah now describes the LORD on His throne with the host of heaven around Him. In the vision, a spirit proposes to entice Ahab by becoming a lying spirit in the mouths of his prophets. The LORD permits the plan to proceed and declares that it will succeed.

Micaiah tells Ahab that this explains the assurances he has received. The LORD has pronounced disaster against him. Ahab hears both the false promise and the warning that exposes it before he chooses to go to battle.

The scene raises a serious question about God’s rule and the lies of others. It should be read alongside Scripture’s direct statements that God cannot lie, in [Titus 1:1–3](https://biblehub.com/bsb/titus/1.htm), and that He does not tempt anyone to evil, in [James 1:13–18](https://biblehub.com/bsb/james/1.htm).
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-kings/) understands the permission as God giving Ahab and the prophets over to their own chosen course. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/22.htm) likewise describes God allowing an evil spirit to work through prophets disposed to flatter the king.

[Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_kings/22.htm) emphasizes that the vision presents heavenly matters in a form people can understand. He cautions against imagining that God needs advice or becomes the author of sin.

The wider traditions agree that God’s rule does not make Him the source of moral evil. The Catholic Church teaches that God permits the evil choices of His creatures and can bring good from them, while remaining entirely good ([Catechism 311–312](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_two/chapter_one/article_1/paragraph_4_the_creator.html)).

Reformed accounts place particular emphasis on God actively limiting and governing evil toward His holy purposes, rather than merely allowing it. Both the [Westminster Confession 5.4](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html) and the [1689 Baptist Confession 5.4](https://www.the1689confession.com/1689/chapter-5) make that distinction while saying that the sin belongs to the creatures, not to God. These statements explain the traditions’ broader approach; they do not identify the unnamed spirit or define every detail of Micaiah’s vision.
god_plan_lines: A related pattern appears in [2 Thessalonians 2:9–12](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_thessalonians/2.htm): people refuse the love of the truth, delight in wickedness and come under a judgment in which they believe a lie. The surrounding passage also announces that the Lord Jesus will bring the lawless one to an end.

The connection is the warning about rejecting truth and embracing deception, not an identification of Ahab with a future figure. In both passages, deception remains under God’s rule and does not give evil the final word.
